## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Colorado [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/colorado.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Colorado [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Colorado residents.

Colorado Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A Colorado resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct Colorado-law implications.

OptionColorado RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPLicensed4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementLicensed (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; Colorado exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

Colorado Debt Consolidation Regulation

Colorado regulates debt consolidation under a licensing/registration regime. (CRS 5-19-101; Administrator of Uniform Consumer Credit Code enforces.) Before signing up with any Colorado DMP, verify the company's license with the named regulator.

Practical Colorado due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Colorado regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Colorado statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Colorado violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in Colorado

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of Colorado law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in Colorado

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Colorado

The Colorado bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Colorado-specific strengths:

Colorado homestead: $250,000 ($350,000 elderly/disabled) (C.R.S. 38-41-201). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Colorado wage protection: 20%. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Colorado auto: $15,000 (38-41-301 since 2022).

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Colorado Federal Bankruptcy Data

When debt consolidation stalls or fails, bankruptcy is the institutional alternative. These FJC numbers show the Colorado bankruptcy landscape.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 86 consumer bankruptcy cases from Colorado's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 78498.8%1.2%

Chapter 132n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Connecticut Debt Consolidation Regulation

Connecticut has strict licensing requirements for debt consolidation companies. (CGS 36a-655 Debt Adjuster Act; Banking Dept oversees; strong consumer protections.) Licensed operators must disclose fees, carry bonds, and follow consumer protection rules. Unlicensed operators face civil and criminal penalties.

Practical Connecticut due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Connecticut regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Connecticut statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Connecticut violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

OptionFlorida RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPLicensed4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementLicensed (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; Florida exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

Florida Debt Consolidation Regulation

Florida regulates debt consolidation under a licensing/registration regime. (Fla. Stat. 817.801 Credit Counseling Services Act; Office of Financial Regulation.) Before signing up with any Florida DMP, verify the company's license with the named regulator.

Practical Florida due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Florida regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Florida statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Florida violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in Florida

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of Florida law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in Florida

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Florida

The Florida bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Florida-specific strengths:

Florida homestead: Unlimited (1/2 acre urban / 160 rural) (Fla. Const. Art. X s.4). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Florida wage protection: 0% (head-of-family under $750/wk). Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Florida auto: $1,000 ($2,000 joint).

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Florida Federal Bankruptcy Data

When debt consolidation stalls or fails, bankruptcy is the institutional alternative. These FJC numbers show the Florida bankruptcy landscape.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 46,008 consumer bankruptcy cases from Florida's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 724,38994.2%5.1%

Chapter 1321,61951.3%48.6%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Florida Numbers Comparison

MetricDMP / SettlementBankruptcy (Ch. 7)

Timeline4-5 years90-120 days

Cost to you$1,500-$6,000 fees + full principal (DMP) or 40-60% principal (settlement)$338 filing fee + $1,500-$3,500 attorney (or pro se $338)

Income requirementMust have steady income for entire termMust pass means test (below Florida median usually passes)

Credit impact-50 to -100 initial; reported for 7 years-100 to -200 initial; stays 10 years but rebuild often faster

Tax consequencesSettled amounts reported on 1099-C (taxable unless insolvent)No tax consequences (IRC 108(a))

Legal protectionNone from lawsuits; creditors may sue mid-planAutomatic stay halts all collection at filing

Asset riskNo asset protection; creditors may attach post-judgmentFlorida homestead + exemptions protect assets

See the full cost calculator and success rates.

Florida Decision Matrix

Use this rough decision tree for Florida residents:

Unsecured debt < 20% of annual income; steady job; no lawsuits pending: DMP may work. Pre-verify Florida license.

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below Florida median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

House behind on payments: Chapter 13 (can cure arrears). DMP doesn't touch mortgage.

See full comparison.

Who Profits from Florida Debt Consolidation?

The economic incentives in Florida debt consolidation are worth understanding:

Nonprofit credit counseling agencies receive fair share contributions (typically 5-15%) from creditors for accounts enrolled in DMPs. The "nonprofit" label does not mean free to you.

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

Law-firm debt settlement has grown; some operate near UPL lines.

Your creditor may prefer a DMP because 100% of principal is recovered vs bankruptcy discharge.

Florida bar complaint authority investigates attorney-affiliated operations that violate rules.

See who profits.

## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Georgia [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/georgia.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Georgia [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Georgia residents.

Georgia Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A Georgia resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct Georgia-law implications.

OptionGeorgia RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPBanned for profit debt adjusters4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementBanned for profit debt adjusters (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; Georgia exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

Georgia Debt Consolidation Regulation

Georgia heavily restricts for-profit debt consolidation / debt settlement services. (OCGA 18-5-1 et seq.; only nonprofit debt adjusters permitted.) This is a consumer-protective posture - the state has decided that debt adjusters pose enough risk that the commercial model is not permitted. Nonprofit credit counseling (often NFCC-affiliated) remains available.

Practical Georgia due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Georgia regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Georgia statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Georgia violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in Georgia

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of Georgia law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

The Georgia bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Georgia-specific strengths:

Georgia homestead: $21,500 ($43,000 joint) (OCGA 44-13-100). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Georgia wage protection: 25%. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Georgia auto: $5,000.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

Illinois auto: $2,400.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Illinois Federal Bankruptcy Data

When debt consolidation stalls or fails, bankruptcy is the institutional alternative. These FJC numbers show the Illinois bankruptcy landscape.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 9,898 consumer bankruptcy cases from Illinois's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 76,72999.5%0.4%

Chapter 133,16945.9%53.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Illinois Numbers Comparison

MetricDMP / SettlementBankruptcy (Ch. 7)

Timeline4-5 years90-120 days

Cost to you$1,500-$6,000 fees + full principal (DMP) or 40-60% principal (settlement)$338 filing fee + $1,500-$3,500 attorney (or pro se $338)

Income requirementMust have steady income for entire termMust pass means test (below Illinois median usually passes)

Credit impact-50 to -100 initial; reported for 7 years-100 to -200 initial; stays 10 years but rebuild often faster

Tax consequencesSettled amounts reported on 1099-C (taxable unless insolvent)No tax consequences (IRC 108(a))

Legal protectionNone from lawsuits; creditors may sue mid-planAutomatic stay halts all collection at filing

Asset riskNo asset protection; creditors may attach post-judgmentIllinois homestead + exemptions protect assets

See the full cost calculator and success rates.

Illinois Decision Matrix

Use this rough decision tree for Illinois residents:

Unsecured debt < 20% of annual income; steady job; no lawsuits pending: DMP may work. Pre-verify Illinois license.

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below Illinois median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

House behind on payments: Chapter 13 (can cure arrears). DMP doesn't touch mortgage.

See full comparison.

Who Profits from Illinois Debt Consolidation?

The economic incentives in Illinois debt consolidation are worth understanding:

Nonprofit credit counseling agencies receive fair share contributions (typically 5-15%) from creditors for accounts enrolled in DMPs. The "nonprofit" label does not mean free to you.

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

Law-firm debt settlement has grown; some operate near UPL lines.

Your creditor may prefer a DMP because 100% of principal is recovered vs bankruptcy discharge.

Illinois bar complaint authority investigates attorney-affiliated operations that violate rules.

See who profits.

## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Indiana [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/indiana.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Indiana [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Indiana residents.

Indiana Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A Indiana resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct Indiana-law implications.

OptionIndiana RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPLicensed4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementLicensed (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; Indiana exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

Indiana Debt Consolidation Regulation

Indiana regulates debt consolidation under a licensing/registration regime. (Ind. Code 28-1-29 Debt Management Company Licensing.) Before signing up with any Indiana DMP, verify the company's license with the named regulator.

Practical Indiana due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Indiana regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Indiana statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Indiana violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in Indiana

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of Indiana law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in Indiana

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Indiana

The Indiana bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Indiana-specific strengths:

Indiana homestead: $22,750 ($45,500 joint) (Ind. Code 34-55-10-2). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Indiana wage protection: 25%. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Indiana auto: Included in $10,250 wildcard.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Indiana Federal Bankruptcy Data

When debt consolidation stalls or fails, bankruptcy is the institutional alternative. These FJC numbers show the Indiana bankruptcy landscape.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 3,325 consumer bankruptcy cases from Indiana's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 779297.5%2.0%

Chapter 132,53369.8%29.5%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Indiana Decision Matrix

Use this rough decision tree for Indiana residents:

Unsecured debt < 20% of annual income; steady job; no lawsuits pending: DMP may work. Pre-verify Indiana license.

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below Indiana median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

House behind on payments: Chapter 13 (can cure arrears). DMP doesn't touch mortgage.

See full comparison.

Who Profits from Indiana Debt Consolidation?

The economic incentives in Indiana debt consolidation are worth understanding:

Nonprofit credit counseling agencies receive fair share contributions (typically 5-15%) from creditors for accounts enrolled in DMPs. The "nonprofit" label does not mean free to you.

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

Law-firm debt settlement has grown; some operate near UPL lines.

Your creditor may prefer a DMP because 100% of principal is recovered vs bankruptcy discharge.

Indiana bar complaint authority investigates attorney-affiliated operations that violate rules.

Cost to you$1,500-$6,000 fees + full principal (DMP) or 40-60% principal (settlement)$338 filing fee + $1,500-$3,500 attorney (or pro se $338)

Income requirementMust have steady income for entire termMust pass means test (below Kentucky median usually passes)

Credit impact-50 to -100 initial; reported for 7 years-100 to -200 initial; stays 10 years but rebuild often faster

Tax consequencesSettled amounts reported on 1099-C (taxable unless insolvent)No tax consequences (IRC 108(a))

Legal protectionNone from lawsuits; creditors may sue mid-planAutomatic stay halts all collection at filing

Asset riskNo asset protection; creditors may attach post-judgmentKentucky homestead + exemptions protect assets

See the full cost calculator and success rates.

Kentucky Decision Matrix

Use this rough decision tree for Kentucky residents:

Unsecured debt < 20% of annual income; steady job; no lawsuits pending: DMP may work. Pre-verify Kentucky license.

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below Kentucky median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

House behind on payments: Chapter 13 (can cure arrears). DMP doesn't touch mortgage.

See full comparison.

Who Profits from Kentucky Debt Consolidation?

The economic incentives in Kentucky debt consolidation are worth understanding:

Nonprofit credit counseling agencies receive fair share contributions (typically 5-15%) from creditors for accounts enrolled in DMPs. The "nonprofit" label does not mean free to you.

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

Law-firm debt settlement has grown; some operate near UPL lines.

Your creditor may prefer a DMP because 100% of principal is recovered vs bankruptcy discharge.

Kentucky bar complaint authority investigates attorney-affiliated operations that violate rules.

See who profits.

## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Louisiana [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/louisiana.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Louisiana [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Louisiana residents.

Louisiana Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A Louisiana resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct Louisiana-law implications.

OptionLouisiana RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPLicensed4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementLicensed (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; Louisiana exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

Louisiana Debt Consolidation Regulation

Louisiana regulates debt consolidation under a licensing/registration regime. (La. R.S. 14:331 Debt Adjusting Business; narrower scope.) Before signing up with any Louisiana DMP, verify the company's license with the named regulator.

Practical Louisiana due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Louisiana regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Louisiana statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Louisiana violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in Louisiana

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of Louisiana law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in Louisiana

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Louisiana

The Louisiana bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Louisiana-specific strengths:

Louisiana homestead: $35,000 (La. R.S. 20:1). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Louisiana wage protection: 25%. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Louisiana auto: $7,500.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Maryland [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/maryland.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Maryland [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maryland residents.

Maryland Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A Maryland resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct Maryland-law implications.

OptionMaryland RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPLicensed (strict)4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementLicensed (strict) (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; Maryland exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

Maryland Debt Consolidation Regulation

Maryland has strict licensing requirements for debt consolidation companies. (Md. Comm. Law 12-901 Debt Management Services Act; OCFR oversight.) Licensed operators must disclose fees, carry bonds, and follow consumer protection rules. Unlicensed operators face civil and criminal penalties.

Practical Maryland due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Maryland regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Maryland statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Maryland violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in Maryland

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of Maryland law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in Maryland

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Maryland

The Maryland bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Maryland-specific strengths:

Maryland homestead: $25,000 (Md. CJP 11-504(f)). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Maryland wage protection: 25% or 30x MW. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Maryland auto: Wildcard only.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Michigan [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/michigan.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Michigan [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Michigan residents.

Michigan Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A Michigan resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct Michigan-law implications.

OptionMichigan RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPLicensed4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementLicensed (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; Michigan exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

Michigan Debt Consolidation Regulation

Michigan regulates debt consolidation under a licensing/registration regime. (MCL 451.411 Debt Management Act.) Before signing up with any Michigan DMP, verify the company's license with the named regulator.

Practical Michigan due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Michigan regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Michigan statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Michigan violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in Michigan

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of Michigan law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in Michigan

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Michigan

The Michigan bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Michigan-specific strengths:

Michigan homestead: $46,125 ($69,200 if 65+/disabled) (MCL 600.5451). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Michigan wage protection: 25%. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Michigan auto: $3,825.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Michigan Federal Bankruptcy Data

When debt consolidation stalls or fails, bankruptcy is the institutional alternative. These FJC numbers show the Michigan bankruptcy landscape.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,133 consumer bankruptcy cases from Michigan's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7633100.0%0.0%

Chapter 1350048.3%51.0%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Michigan Numbers Comparison

MetricDMP / SettlementBankruptcy (Ch. 7)

Timeline4-5 years90-120 days

Cost to you$1,500-$6,000 fees + full principal (DMP) or 40-60% principal (settlement)$338 filing fee + $1,500-$3,500 attorney (or pro se $338)

Income requirementMust have steady income for entire termMust pass means test (below Michigan median usually passes)

Credit impact-50 to -100 initial; reported for 7 years-100 to -200 initial; stays 10 years but rebuild often faster

Tax consequencesSettled amounts reported on 1099-C (taxable unless insolvent)No tax consequences (IRC 108(a))

Legal protectionNone from lawsuits; creditors may sue mid-planAutomatic stay halts all collection at filing

Asset riskNo asset protection; creditors may attach post-judgmentMichigan homestead + exemptions protect assets

See the full cost calculator and success rates.

Michigan Decision Matrix

Use this rough decision tree for Michigan residents:

Unsecured debt < 20% of annual income; steady job; no lawsuits pending: DMP may work. Pre-verify Michigan license.

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below Michigan median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

House behind on payments: Chapter 13 (can cure arrears). DMP doesn't touch mortgage.

See full comparison.

Who Profits from Michigan Debt Consolidation?

The economic incentives in Michigan debt consolidation are worth understanding:

Nonprofit credit counseling agencies receive fair share contributions (typically 5-15%) from creditors for accounts enrolled in DMPs. The "nonprofit" label does not mean free to you.

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

Law-firm debt settlement has grown; some operate near UPL lines.

Your creditor may prefer a DMP because 100% of principal is recovered vs bankruptcy discharge.

Michigan bar complaint authority investigates attorney-affiliated operations that violate rules.

See who profits.

Mississippi Debt Consolidation Regulation

Mississippi heavily restricts for-profit debt consolidation / debt settlement services. (Miss. Code 81-22-1 Debt Management Services Act; nonprofit only.) This is a consumer-protective posture - the state has decided that debt adjusters pose enough risk that the commercial model is not permitted. Nonprofit credit counseling (often NFCC-affiliated) remains available.

Practical Mississippi due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Mississippi regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Mississippi statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Mississippi violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Mississippi auto: $10,000 wildcard.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Montana

The Montana bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Montana-specific strengths:

Montana homestead: $378,560 (MCA 70-32-104). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Montana wage protection: 25%. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Montana auto: $2,500.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Timeline4-5 years90-120 days

Cost to you$1,500-$6,000 fees + full principal (DMP) or 40-60% principal (settlement)$338 filing fee + $1,500-$3,500 attorney (or pro se $338)

Income requirementMust have steady income for entire termMust pass means test (below Montana median usually passes)

Credit impact-50 to -100 initial; reported for 7 years-100 to -200 initial; stays 10 years but rebuild often faster

Tax consequencesSettled amounts reported on 1099-C (taxable unless insolvent)No tax consequences (IRC 108(a))

Legal protectionNone from lawsuits; creditors may sue mid-planAutomatic stay halts all collection at filing

Asset riskNo asset protection; creditors may attach post-judgmentMontana homestead + exemptions protect assets

See the full cost calculator and success rates.

Montana Decision Matrix

Use this rough decision tree for Montana residents:

Unsecured debt < 20% of annual income; steady job; no lawsuits pending: DMP may work. Pre-verify Montana license.

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below Montana median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

House behind on payments: Chapter 13 (can cure arrears). DMP doesn't touch mortgage.

See full comparison.

Who Profits from Montana Debt Consolidation?

The economic incentives in Montana debt consolidation are worth understanding:

Nonprofit credit counseling agencies receive fair share contributions (typically 5-15%) from creditors for accounts enrolled in DMPs. The "nonprofit" label does not mean free to you.

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

Law-firm debt settlement has grown; some operate near UPL lines.

Your creditor may prefer a DMP because 100% of principal is recovered vs bankruptcy discharge.

Montana bar complaint authority investigates attorney-affiliated operations that violate rules.

See who profits.

## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Nebraska [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/nebraska.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Nebraska [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Nebraska residents.

Nebraska Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A Nebraska resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct Nebraska-law implications.

OptionNebraska RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPLicensed4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementLicensed (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; Nebraska exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

Nebraska Debt Consolidation Regulation

Nebraska regulates debt consolidation under a licensing/registration regime. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 69-1201 Debt Management Services Act.) Before signing up with any Nebraska DMP, verify the company's license with the named regulator.

Practical Nebraska due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Nebraska regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Nebraska statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Nebraska violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in Nebraska

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of Nebraska law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in Nebraska

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Nebraska

The Nebraska bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Nebraska-specific strengths:

Nebraska homestead: $60,000 (Neb. Rev. Stat. 40-101). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Nebraska wage protection: 25% / 15% head-of-household. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Nebraska auto: $5,000.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Nevada Debt Consolidation Regulation

Nevada has strict licensing requirements for debt consolidation companies. (NRS 676A Debt Management Services; Financial Institutions Division.) Licensed operators must disclose fees, carry bonds, and follow consumer protection rules. Unlicensed operators face civil and criminal penalties.

Practical Nevada due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Nevada regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Nevada statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Nevada violation.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Legal protectionNone from lawsuits; creditors may sue mid-planAutomatic stay halts all collection at filing

Asset riskNo asset protection; creditors may attach post-judgmentNew Jersey homestead + exemptions protect assets

See the full cost calculator and success rates.

New Jersey Decision Matrix

Use this rough decision tree for New Jersey residents:

Unsecured debt < 20% of annual income; steady job; no lawsuits pending: DMP may work. Pre-verify New Jersey license.

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below New Jersey median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

House behind on payments: Chapter 13 (can cure arrears). DMP doesn't touch mortgage.

See full comparison.

Who Profits from New Jersey Debt Consolidation?

The economic incentives in New Jersey debt consolidation are worth understanding:

Nonprofit credit counseling agencies receive fair share contributions (typically 5-15%) from creditors for accounts enrolled in DMPs. The "nonprofit" label does not mean free to you.

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

Law-firm debt settlement has grown; some operate near UPL lines.

Your creditor may prefer a DMP because 100% of principal is recovered vs bankruptcy discharge.

New Jersey bar complaint authority investigates attorney-affiliated operations that violate rules.

See who profits.

## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in New Mexico [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/new-mexico.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in New Mexico [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Mexico residents.

New Mexico Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A New Mexico resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct New Mexico-law implications.

OptionNew Mexico RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPLicensed4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementLicensed (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; New Mexico exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

New Mexico Debt Consolidation Regulation

New Mexico regulates debt consolidation under a licensing/registration regime. (NMSA 56-2-1 Debt Management Services Act.) Before signing up with any New Mexico DMP, verify the company's license with the named regulator.

Practical New Mexico due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named New Mexico regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some New Mexico statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate New Mexico violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in New Mexico

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of New Mexico law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in New Mexico

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in New Mexico

The New Mexico bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key New Mexico-specific strengths:

New Mexico homestead: $150,000 (NMSA 42-10-9). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

New Mexico wage protection: 25%. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

New Mexico auto: $4,000.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Credit impact-50 to -100 initial; reported for 7 years-100 to -200 initial; stays 10 years but rebuild often faster

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below New Mexico median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

See full comparison.

The economic incentives in New Mexico debt consolidation are worth understanding:

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in New York [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/new-york.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in New York [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New York residents.

New York Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A New York resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct New York-law implications.

OptionNew York RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPNonprofit-only4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementNonprofit-only (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; New York exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

New York Debt Consolidation Regulation

New York heavily restricts for-profit debt consolidation / debt settlement services. (NY Banking Law 579 - only nonprofit budget planners permitted; for-profit DMPs effectively banned.) This is a consumer-protective posture - the state has decided that debt adjusters pose enough risk that the commercial model is not permitted. Nonprofit credit counseling (often NFCC-affiliated) remains available.

Practical New York due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named New York regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some New York statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate New York violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in New York

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of New York law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in New York

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in New York

The New York bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key New York-specific strengths:

New York homestead: $89,975-$179,975 (county-tiered) (CPLR 5206). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

New York wage protection: 10% (CPLR 5231). Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

New York auto: $4,825 ($11,975 hybrid/elec).

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

## Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Ohio [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions
Source: https://debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com/states/ohio.html

← debtconsolidationvsbankruptcy.com home

Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy in Ohio [2026]: DMP Rules + Exemptions

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Ohio Debt Consolidation vs Bankruptcy - The Comparison

A Ohio resident drowning in unsecured debt has three main institutional options: debt management plan (DMP), debt settlement, or bankruptcy. Each has distinct Ohio-law implications.

OptionOhio RuleTypical Outcome

Credit counseling DMPLicensed4-5 year plan at reduced interest; 100% principal repaid

Debt settlementLicensed (same statute usually)2-4 year plan; 40-60% principal; tax and credit consequences

Chapter 7 bankruptcyFederal; Ohio exemptions applyUnsecured debt discharged in 90-120 days

Chapter 13 bankruptcyFederal; 3-5 year planDischarge after plan completion; mortgage cure possible

Ohio Debt Consolidation Regulation

Ohio regulates debt consolidation under a licensing/registration regime. (ORC 4710 Debt Adjusters Act.) Before signing up with any Ohio DMP, verify the company's license with the named regulator.

Practical Ohio due diligence before any DMP / settlement enrollment:

Verify license/registration with the named Ohio regulator.

Check fee disclosures. Some Ohio statutes cap up-front fees; advance-fee debt settlement is a CROA violation federally and often a separate Ohio violation.

Confirm nonprofit status where claimed. IRS 501(c)(3) status does not automatically mean the DMP is reputable; NFCC membership is a better signal.

Request written contract with cancellation rights.

Cross-check with the state AG for open enforcement actions.

Federal CROA Overlay - Applies in Ohio

The federal Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA), 15 U.S.C. Section 1679 et seq., applies on top of Ohio law. Key CROA rules:

No advance fees for debt settlement until at least one debt is settled.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in Ohio

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Ohio

The Ohio bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Ohio-specific strengths:

Ohio homestead: $182,625 (ORC 2329.66(A)(1) (indexed)). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Ohio wage protection: 25%. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Ohio auto: $5,025 (ORC 2329.66).

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Ohio Federal Bankruptcy Data

When debt consolidation stalls or fails, bankruptcy is the institutional alternative. These FJC numbers show the Ohio bankruptcy landscape.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 3,971 consumer bankruptcy cases from Ohio's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 73,53597.7%1.8%

Chapter 1343651.1%48.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Ohio Numbers Comparison

MetricDMP / SettlementBankruptcy (Ch. 7)

Timeline4-5 years90-120 days

Cost to you$1,500-$6,000 fees + full principal (DMP) or 40-60% principal (settlement)$338 filing fee + $1,500-$3,500 attorney (or pro se $338)

Income requirementMust have steady income for entire termMust pass means test (below Ohio median usually passes)

Credit impact-50 to -100 initial; reported for 7 years-100 to -200 initial; stays 10 years but rebuild often faster

Tax consequencesSettled amounts reported on 1099-C (taxable unless insolvent)No tax consequences (IRC 108(a))

Legal protectionNone from lawsuits; creditors may sue mid-planAutomatic stay halts all collection at filing

Asset riskNo asset protection; creditors may attach post-judgmentOhio homestead + exemptions protect assets

See the full cost calculator and success rates.

Ohio Decision Matrix

Use this rough decision tree for Ohio residents:

Unsecured debt < 20% of annual income; steady job; no lawsuits pending: DMP may work. Pre-verify Ohio license.

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below Ohio median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

House behind on payments: Chapter 13 (can cure arrears). DMP doesn't touch mortgage.

See full comparison.

Who Profits from Ohio Debt Consolidation?

The economic incentives in Ohio debt consolidation are worth understanding:

Nonprofit credit counseling agencies receive fair share contributions (typically 5-15%) from creditors for accounts enrolled in DMPs. The "nonprofit" label does not mean free to you.

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

Law-firm debt settlement has grown; some operate near UPL lines.

Your creditor may prefer a DMP because 100% of principal is recovered vs bankruptcy discharge.

Ohio bar complaint authority investigates attorney-affiliated operations that violate rules.

See who profits.

Written contract required with specified disclosures.

3-day right to cancel the contract without penalty.

Prohibition on false / misleading statements about services or results.

Private right of action for consumers harmed by violations.

The FTC also enforces the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) advance-fee ban, which generally prohibits for-profit debt relief companies from collecting fees before settling debts.

Why Debt Consolidation Often Fails in Rhode Island

Income shock. A 4-5 year DMP requires stable income for the entire term. Job loss, medical event, or family emergency ends the plan early - often worse off because interest accrues and creditor accommodations expire.

New debt. Many DMPs require surrender of credit cards; consumers take out new credit to cover emergencies, re-entering the cycle.

Credit damage. DMPs typically require account closure, which lowers credit utilization score and drops FICO by 50-100 points initially.

Tax surprise. Settled debt over $600 is typically reported on 1099-C and treated as taxable income unless insolvency exclusion applies (IRC 108(a)).

Lawsuits mid-plan. Creditors may sue while you are enrolled, creating judgment that adds interest and garnishment risk.

Incomplete coverage. Secured debts (mortgage, car) and non-dischargeables (student loans, taxes, DSO) are not addressed by DMPs.

See when consolidation fails.

Why Bankruptcy Often Wins in Rhode Island

The Rhode Island bankruptcy advantage is protective, not punitive. Key Rhode Island-specific strengths:

Rhode Island homestead: $500,000 (R.I.G.L. 9-26-4.1). Home equity within the exemption is protected.

Rhode Island wage protection: 25%. Garnishment stops at filing and for many earners is limited post-discharge.

Rhode Island auto: $12,000.

Retirement accounts fully protected (ERISA + federal cap).

90-120 day Chapter 7 extinguishes unsecured debt completely.

1099-C exclusion: debt discharged in bankruptcy is NOT taxable income (IRC 108(a)(1)(A)).

Credit reporting: Chapter 7 stays 10 years; Chapter 13 stays 7 years. But FICO rebuild often faster than post-DMP because of clean slate.

See how bankruptcy works and cost comparison.

Rhode Island Numbers Comparison

MetricDMP / SettlementBankruptcy (Ch. 7)

Timeline4-5 years90-120 days

Cost to you$1,500-$6,000 fees + full principal (DMP) or 40-60% principal (settlement)$338 filing fee + $1,500-$3,500 attorney (or pro se $338)

Income requirementMust have steady income for entire termMust pass means test (below Rhode Island median usually passes)

Credit impact-50 to -100 initial; reported for 7 years-100 to -200 initial; stays 10 years but rebuild often faster

Tax consequencesSettled amounts reported on 1099-C (taxable unless insolvent)No tax consequences (IRC 108(a))

Legal protectionNone from lawsuits; creditors may sue mid-planAutomatic stay halts all collection at filing

Asset riskNo asset protection; creditors may attach post-judgmentRhode Island homestead + exemptions protect assets

See the full cost calculator and success rates.

Rhode Island Decision Matrix

Use this rough decision tree for Rhode Island residents:

Unsecured debt < 20% of annual income; steady job; no lawsuits pending: DMP may work. Pre-verify Rhode Island license.

Unsecured debt 20-50% of annual income; job stable but tight: Compare DMP vs Chapter 13 carefully. Chapter 13 fixes plan duration and stops interest.

Unsecured debt > 50% of annual income OR income below Rhode Island median OR any lawsuit pending: Chapter 7 usually better. Run the means test.

Non-consumer debt (business, IRS, student loan) dominant: Standard DMP doesn't help. Chapter 13 or specialized approach.

House behind on payments: Chapter 13 (can cure arrears). DMP doesn't touch mortgage.

See full comparison.

Who Profits from Rhode Island Debt Consolidation?

The economic incentives in Rhode Island debt consolidation are worth understanding:

Nonprofit credit counseling agencies receive fair share contributions (typically 5-15%) from creditors for accounts enrolled in DMPs. The "nonprofit" label does not mean free to you.

For-profit debt settlement companies charge 15-25% of enrolled debt as fees (post-settlement under CROA/TSR).

Law-firm debt settlement has grown; some operate near UPL lines.

Your creditor may prefer a DMP because 100% of principal is recovered vs bankruptcy discharge.

Rhode Island bar complaint authority investigates attorney-affiliated operations that violate rules.

See who profits.
